I am 64 this year, and I have only 6 mu, so I cannot take big risks. I have done wheat-maize for many years, and on this land the safest way is still wheat first, then maize right after harvest. I finished middle school, so I do listen a little to what the extension people say, but in the end I still follow what worked on my own field. Last year if the wheat had decent color and the maize caught the summer rain in time, then I will keep the same pattern, only adjust a little. Fertilizer is expensive, but if I cut too much and the crop turns yellow, that loss is worse for me than spending a bit more. I am alone in the household, so labor must be simple and timing must be tight, especially between wheat harvest and maize sowing. Since I have a well, I will keep irrigation for the key stages, but I will not overwater because pumping costs money.

For wheat, I will sow in early to mid October, using a common improved variety I can buy locally. I will put most fertilizer as base fertilizer, then give one topdressing around jointing if the seedlings look weak or pale. Wheat still needs water more reliably here, so I will plan a few irrigations at overwintering, jointing, and grain filling depending on rain. After wheat harvest in June, I will not waste time with heavy tillage. I will clear the field quickly and plant summer maize right away, because if maize is planted late, yield drops fast. For maize, I will use hybrid seed, put fertilizer a bit lower than wheat, and mostly depend on summer rain, with one or two irrigations only if it turns dry. I will spray herbicide once after sowing or early emergence, and only use insecticide if I actually see pest pressure. This way I keep the system steady, control costs, and make sure the land does not sit idle.
